title: Berkshire 1987 letter: great managers, Mr. Market, buying quality, and conservative debt
summary: Buffett's 1987 letter shows how Berkshire judges businesses by return on capital, hands off great managers, and treats stocks as pieces of businesses while ignoring Mr. Market. It also covers commodity-like insurance economics, why it prefers a fine business at a fair price, capital allocation, and keeping debt low enough to be certain of surviving.

principles.text: Judge a business by growth in per-share business value, not book value, since the two are often unrelated.
principles.quote: What counts, of course, is the rate of gain in per-share business value, not book value.

principles.text: Treat market prices as Mr. Market's offers to serve you, never as guidance; know your business better than he does.
principles.quote: Mr. Market is there to serve you, not to guide you. It is his pocketbook, not his wisdom, that you will find useful.

principles.text: Buy an outstanding business at a sensible price, not a mediocre business at a bargain price.
principles.quote: Our goal is to find an outstanding business at a sensible price, not a mediocre business at a bargain price.

principles.text: Investing success comes from business judgment plus emotional insulation from the market, not arcane formulas.
principles.quote: Rather an investor will succeed by coupling good business judgment with an ability to insulate his thoughts and behavior from the super-contagious emotions that swirl about the marketplace.

principles.text: Stable, unglamorous businesses with strong franchises produce the best returns; constant change invites major error.
principles.quote: Severe change and exceptional returns usually don't mix.

principles.text: Keep debt low enough that survival is certain, not just likely, rather than chase optimal returns with leverage.
principles.quote: But we do not wish it to be only likely that we can meet our obligations; we wish that to be certain.
